newsitem.title: USA: General says U.S. bases will not stay in Panama.
newsitem.headline: General says U.S. bases will not stay in Panama.

text.p: The commander of U.S. forces in South America said flatly on Thursday that the United States would not keep bases in Panama, although its military would participate in a possible counter-drug centre there.

"We're certainly not going to maintain bases down there because we're not going to pay compensation," Gen. Wesley Clark told military writers. "President (Ernesto Perez) Balladares has said ... he's not going to negotiate the bases. I think that's the position," Clark said.

It was one of the strongest statements by a U.S. official on the possibility of keeping U.S. bases after the Panama Canal is turned over to Panama at the end of the century. But officials have said previously that U.S. base rights were no longer being negotiated because of Balladares' public statements against them.

Clark said the counter-drug centre the United States and South American countries are considering in Panama would have a military component and suggested it would be large. He said 80 percent of current U.S. flights out of Howard Air Force Base in Panama are counter-drug flights.

"So essentially the major function that we're performing down there is support of the nations of the region in their fight against narco-trafficking," he said. "So the multilateral counter-drug centre is a very logical follow-on to what is already being done there in Panama."
He said all Panamanian leaders in and out of government he has talked with want to maintain a military relationship with the United States, even if U.S. forces do not stay there.

He also played down Colombia's decision this week to suspend aerial spraying of illicit drug crops, saying U.S. and Colombian officials have continued to cooperate on drug eradication and he was sure any problem could be solved.

Colombian officials told Reuters on Wednesday the spraying had been suspended for a review of its effectiveness, denying it in retaliation for President Bill Clinton's decision last week to extend "decertification" of Colombia's eligibility for U.S. aid because of dissatisfaction with its anti-drug efforts.

Clark said the United States continued to work with Colombia on efforts to curb drug trafficking despite the decertification. He said Colombia was serious about fighting trafficking because of drugs' threat to that country and the rest of the hemisphere.
